solutionSource.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique after crossings); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

entries.clue: No Parisian will accept an extreme emperor (8)

indicatorNotes.will accept: NON takes the other piece inside it, as a host accepts a guest

blocks.note: 'no' as a Parisian says it, in French
A + POLE, an extreme point such as the North Pole

annotation.surface: A Frenchman flatly refuses to put up with some extreme ruler.
annotation.walkthrough: The Parisian is not a person at all; the word just asks for the French for 'no'. 'An extreme' splits as A plus POLE.
annotation.definitionFit: Napoleon Bonaparte crowned himself Emperor of the French in 1804.

entries.clue: Book illustration is perfection in a way (12)

indicatorNotes.in a way: the letters are only 'perfection' in a manner of speaking, i.e. set out another way

annotation.surface: A critic praises a book's picture as flawless, after a fashion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'In a way' reads as a mild hedge on the praise; here it tells you to rearrange all twelve letters of 'is perfection'.
annotation.definitionFit: A frontispiece is the illustration facing a book's title page.

entries.clue: Small item of furniture is not likely to topple (6)

blocks.note: S = small, as on clothing labels
a table is a piece of furniture

annotation.surface: A little side table is sturdy enough not to tip over.
annotation.definitionFit: Something stable is steady and unlikely to fall over.
annotation.walkthrough: Read as a phrase, 'small item of furniture' is a little table; split it, and 'small' gives just its standard abbreviation.

entries.clue: What’s attractive green at first introduced by French artist (6)

indicatorNotes.at first: take only the opening letter of 'green'
indicatorNotes.introduced by: G is brought in by MANET, placed inside his name

annotation.surface: Asks what makes a painting appealing when a Frenchman starts with green.
annotation.walkthrough: 'What's attractive' reads as a question about taste; a magnet is literally attractive. MANET is the crossword's favourite French painter, alongside Monet.
annotation.definitionFit: A magnet attracts iron, so it is quite literally what is attractive.

entries.clue: Girl’s love is knight in shining armour (4)

blocks.note: love = nil = O, from tennis scoring

annotation.surface: A young woman's sweetheart is her gallant rescuer.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'love' as romance; it is the zero of a tennis score.
annotation.definitionFit: An idiom: the knight in shining armour is the gallant rescuer of romance, the story's leading man.

entries.clue: Bird arranged in casserole? (6)

indicatorNotes.in: 'in' as food sits in a pot: ARR is placed inside POT

blocks.note: arr. is the abbreviation for arranged, as on sheet music
a casserole is a cooking pot

annotation.surface: Suggests a bird has been laid out ready for cooking in a stew.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Arranged' looks like an anagram signal, but it is just its abbreviation ARR; the question mark flags that a casserole is the dish, not the stew.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain example: the parrot is the talking bird, a whole family of hookbills.

entries.clue: Accepted a deadly sin (6)

blocks.note: greed is one of the seven deadly sins

annotation.surface: Someone admits to one of the seven deadly sins.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Accepted' seems to describe the sin being committed; it is the definition, meaning consented.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym in the past tense: to have said yes to a proposal.

entries.clue: Only chaps in trade turned out further tailoring (12)

indicatorNotes.in: JUST MEN sits inside the rearranged TRADE
indicatorNotes.turned out: TRADE is turned out, i.e. its letters rearranged

annotation.surface: Only men in the tailoring trade produced more alterations.
annotation.walkthrough: Just the four letters of TRADE are rearranged; JUST MEN goes between READ and T.
annotation.definitionFit: Tailoring is fitting a garment, and doing it again or further is adjusting it anew.

entries.clue: Swindle involving one pound? (4)

indicatorNotes.involving: CON wraps round I, involving it

annotation.surface: A scam that costs its victim just a single pound.
annotation.walkthrough: The pound (the UK currency unit) comes as a coin; the question mark marks it as one example of a coin.
annotation.definitionFit: Definition by example, flagged by the question mark: the British pound is a round metal piece of money.

entries.clue: House in Cork area of little height (8)

blocks.note: a bung is a stopper, like a cork

annotation.surface: A house somewhere in the Irish county of Cork, in a low-lying district.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital C makes Cork look like the Irish county; it is a bottle stopper. Aptly, a bungalow is a single-storey house, so of little height too.
annotation.definitionFit: A bungalow is a house, one built on a single storey.

entries.clue: Living head of state losing power (8)

indicatorNotes.losing: a word that is losing something has a piece taken away: here the P of power goes

blocks.note: a president is a head of state

annotation.surface: A living leader has been stripped of authority.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface asks you to see a head of state lose political power; power is just the letter P.
annotation.definitionFit: Resident means living somewhere, as in 'resident in London'.

entries.clue: Born in want to a large degree (3)

indicatorNotes.to a large degree: to a large degree means mostly, so keep most of the word and drop its last letter

blocks.note: want as in lack or requirement, four letters; drop the D

annotation.surface: Someone was born into great poverty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Born in want' looks like a phrase about poverty; 'in' is only a link, and 'to a large degree' says take most of NEED, the synonym for want.
annotation.definitionFit: Née, French for born, introduces a woman's maiden name.

entries.clue: Fair contest between knights, nought is ruled out (4)

indicatorNotes.is ruled out: the O is struck out of JOUST

blocks.note: a joust is a mounted contest between knights

annotation.surface: A referee rules a fair tournament bout between knights, with no scoring disallowed.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fair' sits by 'contest' like a fair fight, but it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a fair decision is one made in accordance with justice.

entries.clue: Perfectionist staff left Keir regularly (8)

indicatorNotes.regularly: take every other letter of Keir: kEiR

blocks.note: a staff is a walking stick
second and fourth letters of Keir

annotation.surface: A fussy perfectionist's employees walked out on Keir Starmer, the UK Prime Minister.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Staff' and 'left' read as workers quitting; they are a stick and the letter L.
annotation.definitionFit: A stickler insists on everything being exactly right.

entries.clue: Cut nails back (4)

indicatorNotes.back: 'back' as in going backwards: the letters are read from the end to the start

annotation.surface: An instruction to trim your fingernails short.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Cut nails back' reads as manicure advice; the nails are carpentry pins.
annotation.definitionFit: To snip is to cut with small quick strokes.

entries.clue: Carries family headgear (8)

annotation.surface: Someone takes along the family's hats.
annotation.walkthrough: A bearskin is the tall black fur hat worn by the guards outside Buckingham Palace.
annotation.definitionFit: A bearskin is a tall fur cap, a piece of military headgear.

entries.clue: Desperate starlet finally bares chest (6)

indicatorNotes.Desperate: the letters are in a desperate state, i.e. wildly mixed
indicatorNotes.finally: take only the last letter of starlet

annotation.surface: A young actress, desperate for publicity, strips off.
annotation.walkthrough: The tabloid surface keeps 'chest' in plain sight as the definition, at the very end.
annotation.definitionFit: Breast and chest both name the front of the upper body.

entries.clue: Important route for vessel (6)

blocks.note: an arterial road is a main route

annotation.surface: Names a key shipping lane used by a boat.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Vessel' suggests a ship on a route; it is a blood vessel.
annotation.definitionFit: An artery is both a main road or channel and a blood vessel leading from the heart.

entries.clue: In where I am, even parts of units will be built-in (8)

indicatorNotes.even parts of: the even-numbered letters of units: uNiTs

blocks.note: second and fourth letters of units

annotation.surface: Describes components fitted into fixed units where the speaker stands.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like fitted kitchen units; 'even parts' picks out the even letters.
annotation.definitionFit: An inherent quality is built in, part of a thing's nature.

entries.clue: Any number working outside university term? (4)

indicatorNotes.outside: 'outside' puts one piece round the other: N and ON wrap round U

blocks.note: N = any number, as in maths
on = working, as a machine is on

annotation.surface: Asks how many are employed off campus during term time.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Term' reads as a university term; the question mark flags that a noun is only one kind of term, a naming word.
annotation.definitionFit: A noun is a word or term naming a thing.

entries.clue: Earn millions as keen entrepreneur initially (4)

indicatorNotes.initially: take the first letters of as keen entrepreneur

blocks.note: first letters of as, keen, entrepreneur

annotation.surface: A keen entrepreneur rakes in millions.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: to earn a salary is to bring in money, as in 'making a living'.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Initially' could apply to 'entrepreneur' alone; here it covers all three words before it, while 'millions' contributes its standard abbreviation.

entries.clue: Compulsion to put on clothes over uniform (6)

indicatorNotes.over: DRESS goes over, i.e. covers, U

blocks.note: to dress = to put on clothes
U = uniform in the NATO phonetic alphabet

annotation.surface: Someone feels obliged to put a coat on over their uniform.
annotation.walkthrough: The clothes and uniform picture hides the plain wordplay: DRESS placed over U.
annotation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: compulsion is being forced by threats, a legal defence term.

entries.clue: Shoot messenger (6)

blocks.note: a shoot in the botanical sense: a creeping stem, as on strawberries
one who carries messages, especially on foot

annotation.surface: The old warning not to shoot the messenger.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface echoes 'don't shoot the messenger', making 'Shoot' look like a verb; it is a noun, a plant's shoot.
annotation.definitionFit: A runner is both a creeping stem that roots new plants and someone who carries messages.
